title: NURS 1017 Unit 7 Case Study 7
description: 64-year-old female client at a community health clinic who reports a resolved episode of right-hand weakness and jumbled speech: recognizing a TIA, modifiable and non-modifiable stroke risk factors, same-day emergency referral, FAST teaching, anticoagulant and antihypertensive teaching, and evaluation of secondary prevention.

authorReview.note:
New case written by Claude on 2 Nov 2026 for the Unit 7 learning outcomes; please review before using it with students:
- Nursing-focused case (assessment, priorities, teaching, evaluation), following OpenStax 15.2 for TIA and stroke prevention.
- Referral pathway follows the Canadian Stroke Best Practice Recommendations (same-day emergency assessment for a TIA with weakness or speech symptoms within 48 hours).
- Clinician review: the missed-dose rule for apixaban and the BP target after TIA.

question.explanation:
Require follow-up:

Sudden one-sided hand weakness and numbness with jumbled speech that cleared in 15 minutes: these are stroke warning signs. Even though they have gone, the nurse treats them as a possible transient ischemic attack (TIA) and records when they started and stopped (last known well: before 0730).

Irregular pulse: may be atrial fibrillation, a common source of clots that travel to the brain; the nurse counts the apical pulse for a full minute and reports it.

BP 172/96 mm Hg after stopping amlodipine: uncontrolled hypertension is the most important modifiable stroke risk factor. Stopping a medication because of a side effect without telling the provider is a teaching need.

Smoking: a modifiable risk factor that damages blood vessels and makes blood clot more easily.

Do not require follow-up now: her normal neurological assessment today (alert, clear speech, symmetrical smile, equal grips), temperature, respirations, oxygen saturation and capillary glucose. A normal glucose also rules out hypoglycemia as the cause of the episode.

question.stem: The nurse identifies the client's risk factors for stroke. For each risk factor, click to specify whether it is modifiable or non-modifiable.

rows.text: Type 2 diabetes with an HbA1c of 8.6%

question.explanation:
Why risk factors matter after a TIA: a TIA is a temporary blockage of blood flow to part of the brain; the clot clears on its own, so the symptoms resolve without permanent damage. It is a warning: the risk of a stroke in the next 90 days is high (about 18%), and it is greatest in the first 48 hours. Teaching aims at the factors the client can change.

Modifiable (can be treated or changed): hypertension, smoking, physical inactivity, diabetes (glucose control), obesity, unhealthy diet, high cholesterol, heavy alcohol use, sleep apnea, and atrial fibrillation (treated with anticoagulation and rate control).

Non-modifiable: age, family history, sex, race and ethnicity, and a previous stroke or TIA. These cannot be changed, but they raise the client's overall risk, so the modifiable factors matter even more.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The client's episode is most consistent with [[drop0]]. The nurse's priority is the client's [[drop1]], so the nurse [[drop2]].

options.text: anxiety
a hypoglycemic reaction
a migraine
a transient ischemic attack
knowledge of a healthy diet
high risk of a stroke in the next few days
need for a smoking cessation plan
ankle swelling from amlodipine
arranges for her to be assessed in an emergency department today
books a follow-up appointment with her primary care provider next week
teaches her to rest and call the clinic if the symptoms return
restarts her amlodipine from her supply at home

question.explanation:
Transient ischemic attack: sudden focal symptoms (one-sided weakness and numbness, speech disturbance) that resolved completely within minutes, with a normal glucose, fit a TIA rather than hypoglycemia, migraine or anxiety.

Priority: the risk of a disabling stroke is highest in the first 48 hours after a TIA, especially when the symptoms included weakness or speech problems. Canadian stroke guidelines direct these clients to an emergency department the same day for brain and vessel imaging, an ECG for atrial fibrillation, and prompt preventive treatment. Diet, smoking and the medication side effect are all important, but they come after this immediate safety need.

Why not the others: waiting a week for an appointment loses the window when preventive treatment helps most. Restarting a medication is a provider decision. Telling her to call the clinic delays care; if symptoms return, she calls 9-1-1.

question.stem: The provider agrees that the client should go to the emergency department now. Which actions should the nurse include before she leaves the clinic? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give her an aspirin from the clinic supply to take on the way
Teach her and her daughter the FAST signs of stroke and to call 9-1-1 if any return
Tell her she should not drive herself to the emergency department
Send a list of her medications, including the amlodipine she stopped
Ask her to come back to the clinic tomorrow if she still feels well
Phone a report to the emergency department nurse
Write down the time the symptoms started and when they resolved
Reassure her that no further testing is needed because her symptoms are gone

question.explanation:
Include: a new neurological event can recur on the way, so she does not drive. The times of onset and resolution guide the emergency team (and would determine eligibility for clot-dissolving treatment if a stroke followed). FAST (Heart & Stroke Foundation of Canada): Face drooping, Arm weakness (cannot raise both arms), Speech jumbled or slurred, Time to call 9-1-1 right away; she and her family must not wait to see whether symptoms pass. A medication list and a nurse-to-nurse report support safe handover of care.

Do not include: aspirin is not given until a hemorrhage has been ruled out and a provider prescribes it. Resolved symptoms do not mean she is safe; she needs assessment today. Waiting until tomorrow delays care in the highest-risk period.

question.stem: For each teaching point, click to specify whether the nurse should include it or not include it in the client's teaching.

rows.text: Take apixaban twice a day, about 12 hours apart, every day
If you miss a dose of apixaban, take two tablets at the next dose
Report black stools, blood in the urine, or bleeding gums that do not stop
Use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor
Check with the pharmacist before taking any herbal products or supplements
Stop the perindopril on your own if you develop a dry cough
Ask about the free smoking cessation program and nicotine replacement

question.explanation:
Include: apixaban protects against clots from atrial fibrillation only if it is taken regularly; it is taken twice a day about 12 hours apart. It increases bleeding risk, so the client learns the signs of bleeding to report and uses a soft toothbrush and an electric razor. Many herbal products (for example, ginkgo, garlic and St. John's wort) change bleeding risk or drug levels. Stopping smoking is one of the most effective ways to lower stroke risk; provincial cessation programs offer counselling and nicotine replacement.

Do not include: a missed apixaban dose is taken as soon as it is remembered on the same day, then the usual schedule continues; doses are never doubled. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen add to bleeding risk; acetaminophen is preferred. Stopping her antihypertensive on her own is what happened with the amlodipine; she reports side effects (an ACE inhibitor can cause a dry cough) so the provider can change the drug.

question.explanation:
Outcomes met: her BP is now within the target (below 130/80 mm Hg for most people after a stroke or TIA), she has stopped smoking, she is active on most days, and she can recognize stroke signs and knows to call 9-1-1.

Require follow-up: missed apixaban doses leave her unprotected against clots from atrial fibrillation; the nurse explores the reason and suggests strategies (phone alarm, pill organizer, linking the dose to supper) and informs the provider. An HbA1c of 8.4% is above the usual target of 7% or lower, so diabetes management (diet, activity, medications, follow-up with the diabetes educator) needs attention.
